# Model card: CreditRisk PD model

## Read this first
**All numbers below come from SYNTHETIC data** (generated by `data.generate_synthetic`, seed 42). They validate that the
pipeline works; they are **not** evidence of performance on real borrowers and are not comparable with Kaggle leaderboards.
Real Kaggle data has not been run through this code. Model version: `20261101-100143`.

## Intended use
Educational/portfolio demonstration of an explainable credit decision pipeline for unsecured consumer lending.
**Not** approved for real credit decisions. A production use would need real data, legal review of fair-lending rules,
out-of-time validation, independent model validation and authentication on the service.

## Data
Synthetic, 60,000 rows, same schema as Kaggle "Give Me Some Credit"; 7.03% defaults; ~20% missing income; outliers and
96/98 codes injected. Stratified split: train 36,000 / validation 12,000 / test 12,000 (seed 42).
Defaults are generated from a latent stress factor plus a logistic rule, including a mild age effect (younger = riskier).
Cleaning rules and features: [data_dictionary.md](data_dictionary.md).

## Models
- **Scorecard**: quantile WoE bins (<= 8, each >= 5% of rows), features with IV >= 0.02 (9 of 13), logistic regression, points per bin
  (base 600 at 50:1, PDO 20). Unweighted (WoE inputs keep it well calibrated).
- **Gradient boosting**: scikit-learn `GradientBoostingClassifier` (200 trees, depth 3, learning rate 0.05, subsample 0.8),
  balanced sample weights.
- Both are Platt-calibrated on the validation set. **The API uses gradient boosting.**
- **Imbalance handling**: stratified splits; sample weights for boosting; calibration to undo the probability inflation caused by
  weighting; evaluation with rank/precision metrics rather than accuracy (a model that approves everyone is 93% "accurate" and useless).

## Test-set metrics (12,000 rows, 843 defaults)
| Metric | Scorecard | Gradient boosting |
|---|---|---|
| ROC-AUC | 0.7691 | 0.7680 |
| Gini | 0.5382 | 0.5360 |
| KS | 0.4148 | 0.4087 |
| PR-AUC (base rate 0.0703) | 0.2415 | 0.2524 |
| Brier | 0.0593 | 0.0590 |

The models tie. This is a property of the synthetic generator (near-linear), not a general finding.

**Calibration, gradient boosting, by PD decile (test set; `reports/calibration_gb.csv`)**
| Decile | Mean predicted PD | Observed default rate |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 0.0068 | 0.0133 |
| 2 | 0.0122 | 0.0158 |
| 3 | 0.0202 | 0.0208 |
| 4 | 0.0290 | 0.0308 |
| 5 | 0.0386 | 0.0450 |
| 6 | 0.0507 | 0.0408 |
| 7 | 0.0650 | 0.0592 |
| 8 | 0.0851 | 0.0983 |
| 9 | 0.1252 | 0.1125 |
| 10 | 0.2576 | 0.2658 |

The largest per-decile gap is about 1.3 percentage points (decile 8); the lowest-risk decile is slightly under-predicted (0.7% vs 1.3%).
Plots: `reports/roc_and_calibration.png`. Scorecard calibration: `reports/calibration_scorecard.csv`.

## Decisions
Costs (config): cost of an approved default 10,000; profit lost by declining a good customer 1,000; REFER band = 40% of the decline cut-off.
Resulting cut-offs on validation: **APPROVE if PD < 0.0388; DECLINE if PD >= 0.0971; otherwise REFER**
(the analytic break-even for a perfectly calibrated model is 1000/11000 = 0.0909).
On the test set: approve 45.5% / refer 33.8% / decline 20.7%; default rate among approved 2.3%, among declined 18.8%;
expected cost 5.78M vs 8.43M for approving everyone. These costs are placeholders, not bank data.

## Explainability
SHAP `TreeExplainer` on the gradient boosting model (log-odds scale). For REFER/DECLINE the top positive-SHAP features are turned into
sentences ("Revolving credit utilization is very high (98%)"); negative contributors are never listed as decline reasons.
For APPROVE the strongest risk-reducing factors are shown. The scorecard gives an additive points breakdown per applicant (`demo.py`).
SHAP is relative to the average applicant and for interacting features can occasionally yield a reason that feels surprising; it is
an attribution of the model, not causal advice.

## Fairness and governance
- **Age is excluded from the model** because lending regulations (for example ECOA / Regulation B in the US; rules differ by country)
  restrict using age in credit decisions. Age is accepted by the API and stored only for monitoring.
- Features that may correlate with age (income, number of credit lines) are still used: proxy risk is not eliminated.

Age-group check on the test set (gradient boosting, `reports/fairness_by_age_group.csv`):
| Age group | n | Actual default rate | Mean predicted PD | ROC-AUC | Approve rate | Decline rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| <25 | 359 | 12.3% | 7.0% | 0.758 | 43.5% | 22.3% |
| 25-34 | 1,131 | 10.7% | 6.9% | 0.740 | 45.1% | 21.8% |
| 35-49 | 3,711 | 8.5% | 6.9% | 0.766 | 46.6% | 20.6% |
| 50-64 | 4,342 | 6.1% | 6.9% | 0.795 | 44.8% | 21.0% |
| 65+ | 2,457 | 3.9% | 6.8% | 0.754 | 45.4% | 19.6% |

Reading: approval rates are similar across groups (43-47%) and discrimination (AUC) is similar (0.74-0.80; the <25 group is small).
But because the model cannot see age, it **under-predicts risk for young borrowers and over-predicts for older borrowers** in this
synthetic data (mean PD flat at ~7% while actual default rates fall from 12% to 4%). That is the intended price of excluding age,
and a governance team would want to know it. Whether it is acceptable is a policy decision, not a modelling one.

## Monitoring plan
- **PSI per feature** against the training distribution (`python -m creditrisk.drift`): < 0.10 stable, 0.10-0.25 investigate, > 0.25 act.
  Requires >= 100 stored applications. Illustration (`reports/psi_*.csv`): test vs train, all features < 0.01;
  a simulated shift (utilization x1.5, income x0.7) gives MonthlyIncome PSI 0.71 (ALERT) and utilization PSI 0.21 (WARN).
- Monthly: Gini/KS and calibration on matured outcomes (outcomes arrive ~2 years after origination, so use early-delinquency proxies in practice).
- Approval/refer/decline mix and average score; alert on sudden change.
- Retrain when PSI alerts or performance decays; candidate compared on a fixed test set; humans promote.

## Limitations
Synthetic data; random (not out-of-time) split; no reject inference; non-monotone scorecard bins; correlated engineered features;
cost assumptions invented; Platt calibration assumes a stable relationship; no confidence interval on metrics (843 defaults gives AUC standard error of roughly 0.01);
retraining on a handful of feedback rows only adds noise.
